Received June 16, 2026; accepted October 6, 2026 Abstract Context. Dwarf early–type galaxies (ETGs) are abundant in nearby clusters and provide a key laboratory for studying environmentally driven galaxy transformation. Although dwarf ETGs were once considered structurally simple, deep imaging has revealed embedded spiral-like features (e.g., bars and spiral arms) in some of them, contributing only a small fraction of the total galaxy light. The origin of these features at dwarf scales remains uncertain. Aims. As a pilot study, we investigate the nature of spiral-like features in nine Virgo dwarf ETGs with clear embedded arms. Our goal is to use optical colors to test whether these features differ from the surrounding diffuse component, which would constrain their formation pathways. In doing so we establish the methodology on a well-characterized sample, ahead of a future analysis of the much larger NGVS dwarf sample. Methods. Using deep g g - and i i -band images from the NGVS, we apply a residual-based image analysis method to separate excess light associated with the spiral-like component from the diffuse host. The residual images are used to define the arm and interarm regions, enabling direct measurements of light fractions and g − i g-i colors for the spiral-like feature and the diffuse component in which they are embedded. Results. The spiral-like features contribute only a few percent of the total galaxy light (approximately 1.5 % − 5.5 % 1.5\%\!-\!5.5\% in i i and 1.7 % − 3.7 % 1.7\%\!-\!3.7\% in g g ). We find a diverse range of stellar colors across the sample: four galaxies host spiral-like features that are redder than their interarm regions, four show no robust color difference between the arm and interarm regions, and one exhibits a distinctly bluer spiral-like component. The latter is consistent with a recently quenched transition object, while the redder and color-uniform features are consistent with an older or more metal-rich stellar population. Conclusions. Spiral-like features in Virgo dwarf ETGs exhibit a surprising diversity in their photometric properties, implying multiple evolutionary channels are at work rather than a single one. This pilot analysis also demonstrates the readiness for the much larger NGVS sample of dwarfs with potential spiral-like features. Key Words. Galaxies: dwarf – Galaxies: elliptical and lenticular, cD – Galaxies: clusters: individual: Virgo Cluster – Galaxies: structure – Galaxies: evolution – Techniques: image processing 1 Introduction In the local Universe, small, low-mass dwarf galaxies represent the most numerous class of galaxies ( Binggeli et al., 1985 ; Ferguson, 1989 ) . Morphologically, dwarfs are commonly divided into two broad categories based on their global colors and level of star formation activity ( Sandage and Binggeli, 1984 ) : dwarf early–type galaxies (dETGs) and dwarf late-type galaxies (dLTGs). Both are characterized by low luminosities with the bright end being M B ≈ − 18 M_{B}\approx-18 ( Ferguson and Binggeli, 1994 ) and low stellar masses ( M ⋆ ≲ 10 9 − 9.5 ​ M ⊙ M_{\star}\lesssim 10^{9-9.5}\,{\rm M_{\odot}} ). Dwarf LTGs exhibit blue colors, ongoing star formation, and substantial reservoirs of gas and dust. They typically show irregular morphologies ( e.g., Carignan and Beaulieu 1989 ; Skillman et al. 1989 ; Conselice et al. 2003 ; Skillman 2005 ; Ann et al. 2015 ) or spiral-like features containing spiral arms or bars (e.g., Grebel 2001 ) and they are preferentially located in the lower-density outskirts of galaxy clusters, where dwarfs tend to rotate more strongly than those in the inner cluster. In contrast, dwarf ETGs are largely quenched systems with little gas or dust, resulting in their globally red optical colors and generally smooth morphology. Historically divided into dwarf ellipticals ( Ferguson and Binggeli, 1994 ; Graham and Guzmán, 2003 ) , dwarf lenticulars ( Sandage and Binggeli, 1984 ; Binggeli and Cameron, 1991 ) , and dwarf spheroidals ( Harbeck et al., 2001 ) , dwarf ETGs dominate the galaxy population in dense environments ( Binggeli et al., 1985 ; Kurzner et al., 2025 ) , while their occurrence in the field is very rare, with a probability below ∼ 0.06 % \sim 0.06\% ( Geha et al., 2012 ) . Dwarf ETGs, despite their seemingly simple appearance, have been discovered to harbor a range of intricate structural and stellar population complexities. Many are not well described by a single Sersic profile ( Sersic, 1968 ) , exhibiting multiple components ( Janz et al., 2012 ; Janz et al., 2014 ; Su et al., 2021 ) ; moreover, spiral arms and bars have been detected in several cluster ETGs ( Jerjen et al., 2001 ; Barazza et al., 2002 ; De Rijcke et al., 2003 ; Graham and Guzmán, 2003 ; Ferrarese et al., 2006 ; Lisker et al., 2006c ; Penny et al., 2014 ; Venhola et al., 2019 ; Michea et al., 2022 ) . Color imaging has revealed that some of these galaxies contain blue central regions indicative of recent or ongoing star formation, even though the class as a whole resides on the red sequence of the color–magnitude diagram ( Hodge, 1973 ; Vigroux et al., 1984 ; Peletier, 1993 ; Lisker et al., 2006b ; Pak et al., 2014 ; Urich et al., 2017 ; Hamraz et al., 2019 ) . These "blue-cored" dwarf ETGs are preferentially located in the lower-density outskirts of galaxy clusters where dwarfs tend to be rotating more strongly than dwarf in the inner cluster ( Lisker, 2009 ; Toloba et al., 2009 ) . Almost all ETGs have negative metallicity gradients ( Urich et al., 2017 ; Sybilska et al., 2017 ; Bidaran et al., 2023 ) . Some of these steep gradients are linked to past dwarf-dwarf merger events ( Taibi et al., 2022 ) , while others are associated with the presence of shells in certain cluster members ( Paudel et al., 2017 ) . Evidence of morphological and stellar population diversity implies that dwarf ETGs do not originate from a single progenitor, but instead emerge through multiple evolutionary pathways (see Lisker, 2009 ). In the literature, these pathways are generally grouped into two broad classes: "nature" and "nurture" scenarios. In the nature scenario, the properties of dwarf ETGs reflect their intrinsic formation histories, such as early collapse, gradual mass assembly, or minor mergers that can heat or reshape their stellar components. In nurture, environmental mechanisms acting after infall into a group or cluster are responsible for quenching star formation and transforming LTG progenitors into ETGs. Several processes can contribute to such transformations, including starvation or strangulation, which halts the supply of fresh gas as the galaxy falls into high-density regions ( Larson et al., 1980 ; Boselli et al., 2008 ) ; ram-pressure stripping by the hot intracluster medium, which efficiently removes cold gas ( Gunn and Gott, 1972 ; van Zee et al., 2004 ; De Rijcke et al., 2010 ) ; and tidal harassment from high-speed encounters or the global cluster potential, which primarily leads to dynamical heating and thickening of stellar disks ( Smith et al., 2010 ; Smith et al., 2015 ) and can perturb internal structures ( Moore et al., 1998 ; Moore et al., 1999 ; Michea et al., 2022 ) . Early systematic efforts, most notably by Lisker et al. (2006c) , used an iterative technique similar to unsharp masking on SDSS imaging to identify and study spiral-like substructures such as bars and spiral arms in Virgo dwarf ETGs. These studies first established that a nonnegligible fraction of Virgo dwarf galaxies exhibit embedded spiral-like components, and that residual-based decomposition can delineate where those components lie within a galaxy. While their contribution to the total galaxy light is typically modest (between 5 % 5\% – 15 % 15\% ), it can rise to nearly half in some dwarf ETGs. A more refined approach was introduced by Michea et al. (2021) , who formalized and extended these residual-based techniques into an iterative procedure, referred to as the "residual method", applied to nine Virgo dwarf ETGs with prior evidence of embedded substructures in SDSS DR4 imaging ( Lisker et al., 2006c ) . Using deep white-light wide field imager (WFI) imaging, they find that the hidden structures contribute between 2.2 % 2.2\% and 6.4 % 6.4\% of the total galaxy light within two effective radii ( R e R_{\mathrm{e}} ). However, the use of a single broad white filter meant that little information could be recovered on the stellar populations of the hidden spiral-like features, leaving open the question of whether they differ from the main body of the galaxy. With deep multiwavelength photometry it becomes possible to search for color differences between the spiral-like features and their host galaxy. The presence of such differences would demonstrate that the two components host distinct stellar populations, and would already begin to place constraints on the origin of the features. The well-known age–metallicity degeneracy, however, means that a color difference alone cannot reveal whether it arises from a difference in age, in metallicity, or in both, and answering that question will ultimately require spectroscopy. Deep multiwavelength imaging is nevertheless of considerable value to spectroscopic studies in its own right. Dwarf galaxies are intrinsically faint and of low surface brightness, which already makes spectroscopy expensive, and the spiral-like features of interest typically contribute only a few percent of the total galaxy light, so that they are swamped by the light of the main stellar body. Deep imaging combined with the iterative residual method can identify the objects of interest, pinpoint the exact locations of the spiral-like features, and thereby provide crucial constraints on where to place spectroscopic slits or which IFU spaxels to stack. It also measures the fraction of light contained in the arms, which allows the feasibility of a spectroscopic study to be assessed and integration times to be estimated, while the broadband colors offer an educated guess as to whether emission lines are likely to be present. We therefore regard deep multiwavelength imaging, combined with the residual method, as a crucial prerequisite,or at the very least a highly valuable preliminary step, toward successful spectroscopic studies of these objects. The majority of dwarf ETGs with spiral-like features that have been found and studied belong to the Virgo cluster, owing to its proximity ( Blakeslee et al., 2009 , approximately 16.5 16.5\, Mpc;) and to the fact that it has been extensively cataloged and surveyed; see, the Virgo Cluster Catalog ( Binggeli et al., 1985 , VCC;) ; the Advanced Camera for Surveys Virgo Cluster Survey ( Côté et al., 2004 ) ; The Next Generation Virgo Cluster Survey ( Ferrarese et al., 2012 , NGVS;) . However, the origin of these spiral-like features is still an object of scientific debate. It is often suggested that dwarf ETGs are the remnants of infalling dwarf LTGs that were quenched by environmental transformation ( Moore et al., 1998 ; Penny et al., 2014 ) . Another possibility, not necessarily mutually exclusive, is that the environment may trigger the formation of these features in dwarf ETGs; Smith et al. (2021) used high-resolution simulations of cluster harassment and find that spiral-like features, like bars and spiral arms, can arise when a rotationally supported, dynamically cold stellar disk is embedded within a thicker, hotter component. Tidal interactions with the cluster potential can then trigger the formation of spiral arms and bar features, even in the absence of star formation. In this work we present a pilot color analysis of hidden spiral-like features in Virgo dwarf ETGs based on deep multiband NGVS imaging ( Ferrarese et al., 2012 ) , providing optical color information at a depth comparable to Michea et al. (2021) . We deliberately revisit the same nine galaxies analyzed by Michea et al. (2021) with a primary goal of measuring the optical color ( g − i g-i ) of hidden spiral-like features. With this calibrated technique in hand, we use the residual method to isolate the location of spiral-like features (arms, bars, and disks), measure their light fractions and g − i g-i colors and compare them to those of the surrounding diffuse host. The aim is to test whether these embedded features exhibit systematic color differences relative to the main body. Such a test bears directly on the nature and nurture scenarios outlined above. If the features are the recently transformed descendants of infalling dwarf LTGs ( Moore et al., 1998 ; Penny et al., 2014 ) , the arms which hosted the bulk of the star formation prior to quenching should appear bluer than the diffuse body ( Lisker et al., 2006c ; Pak et al., 2014 ; Urich et al., 2017 ) . However, if the quenching occurred sufficiently long ago, the blue arms may fade to red colors, becoming similar in color to the diffuse component. Alternatively, Smith et al. (2021) proposed that a high rotation support/dynamically cold disk can be tidally triggered to form bars and spiral features without triggering the dynamically hotter surrounding disk. In this scenario, a thin cold disk might hide within the dominating thick disk, only revealing itself after a strong tidal shock such as a cluster pericenter passage. If the thin disk is also old and red, having hidden for a long time, the colors of the spiral features that are generated might be indistinguishable from the diffuse component. Finally, if the spiral-like feature is more metal-rich than its surroundings as reported for the central regions of some Virgo dwarf ETGs ( Urich et al., 2017 ; Bidaran et al., 2022 ) , the features should appear redder at comparable age. Broadband colors alone cannot break the age–metallicity degeneracy (Sect. 5 ), but they can establish which regime each galaxy occupies. This paper is organized as follows. Sect. 2 describes the sample selection, the NGVS data, the preprocessing steps and the global properties of the sample. Sect. 3 presents the residual method ( Michea et al., 2021 ) , its multiband extension ( Michea et al., 2022 ) , the revised jump-out criterion introduced in this work and the resulting residual light fractions. Sect. 4 reports the g − i g-i color measurements of the spiral-like features and the accompanying significance analysis. In Sect. 5 we interpret the results in the context of formation channels and environmental processing and Sect. 6 summarizes our conclusions. 2 Data and observations 2.1 Sample selection This work is based on g g - and i i -band imaging from NGVS ( Ferrarese et al., 2012 ) , the deepest wide-field optical survey of the Virgo cluster to date. The NGVS covers 104 ​ deg 2 104\penalty\ \mathrm{deg}^{2} around the two main subclusters centered on M87 and M49, reaching a 2 ​ σ 2\sigma limiting surface brightness of μ g ≃ 29 ​ mag ​ arcsec − 2 \mu_{g}\simeq 29\;\mathrm{mag\,arcsec^{-2}} for extended emission. To minimize contamination from interloping foreground stars and background galaxies, we used a bad pixel mask (BPM), described in Ferrarese et al. (2020, Sect. 5.1.1) . We matched the point-spread functions (PSFs) of the g − g- and i − i- band images using a cross-convolution scheme, convolving each band with the PSF model of the other. The advantage of this approach is operational: it equalizes the effective resolution of the two bands without requiring an analytical or fitted target PSF, removing one possible source of systematic error in the color maps. The trade-off is that both images are degraded to an effective resolution slightly worse than that of either original band. We then fitted galaxy isophotes to the PSF-matched images with the IRAF ELLIPSE task, allowing the center position, ellipticity, and position angle to vary freely with the semimajor axis. The BPM was supplied to ELLIPSE so that contaminated pixels are excluded from the fitting. We defined the galaxy boundary as the outermost isophote whose mean intensity lies at least 2 ​ σ 2\sigma above the background noise level. We estimated the background using SExtractor ( Bertin and Arnouts, 1996 ) BACKGROUND and BACKGROUND RMS images, with a mesh size ( BACK_SIZE ) of 64 pixels 2 . All magnitudes and surface brightnesses reported in this work are in the AB system and have been corrected for Galactic foreground extinction using the reddening maps of Schlafly and Finkbeiner (2011) , with extinction coefficients A g / E ⁡ ( B − V ) = 3.560 A_{g}/E(B{-}V)=3.560 and A i / E ⁡ ( B − V ) = 1.813 A_{i}/E(B{-}V)=1.813 derived from the Fitzpatrick (1999) extinction law via the York Extinction Solver. 2.3 Structural parameters From the PSF-matched isophotal profiles we derived the structural and photometric properties of the sample. we measured total flux within the outermost valid isophote (defined in Sect. 2.2 ) and defined the effective radius R e R_{\mathrm{e}} as the semimajor axis of the isophote enclosing half of this total flux. The resulting photometric properties are listed in columns 4 and 5 of Table 1 . We note that the exact magnitudes can differ slightly from those reported by other studies using NGVS data, owing to differences in the adopted photometric measurement choices. The galaxies are intrinsically faint, with absolute magnitudes in the range − 18.76 ≤ M i ≤ − 16.98 -18.76\leq M_{i}\leq-16.98 and relatively uniform average colors of 0.74 ≤ ( g − i ) ≤ 0.97 0.74\leq(g{-}i)\leq 0.97 mag, consistent with a sample of low-luminosity, moderately red dwarf galaxies. The galaxy center was defined as the centroid of the isophote at a semimajor axis of 1.5 × PSF FWHM 1.5\times\mathrm{PSF}_{\mathrm{FWHM}} , which prevents any effect of the PSF when determining the central coordinates. The area enclosed by this isophote was masked and added to the BPM to alleviate contamination from unresolved nuclear light in subsequent analyses; this also prevents fitting artifacts that the ELLIPSE task can produce in the steep central gradient. The masked region represents a negligible fraction of the effective radius, so no significant galaxy light is lost. These measurements define the reference geometry used to configure the residual method described in Sect. 3 . 3 The residual method The residual method, introduced by Michea et al. (2021) , is an iterative image-analysis procedure designed to separate a galaxy image into two distinct components: (i) a galaxy model image that contains the dominant, smooth (axisymmetric) light of the diffuse stellar body, and (ii) a galaxy residual image that contains the secondary, nonaxisymmetric light associated with embedded substructures such as spiral arms and bars. The procedure works as follows. The galaxy image is first convolved with an elliptical Gaussian kernel (using the IRAF.GAUSS task) whose shape matches the global geometry of the galaxy at two effective radii. The kernel size is tuned to blur out the spiral-like features while preserving the overall light distribution. The smoothed image is then fitted with concentric, free–ellipticity isophotes ( IRAF.ELLIPSE ), yielding a geometric description of the radial light profile that is minimally influenced by the substructures. These isophotes are subsequently imposed on the original (unsmoothed) galaxy image in photometry-only mode to recover the true average brightness along each contour. From these measurements a two-dimensional model of the diffuse component is built with IRAF.BMODEL , and subtracting this model from the original image produces the galaxy residual image, which ideally isolates the spiral-like component light. In practice, however, some light from the spiral-like features inventively contaminates the model after a single-pass, causing the residual image to suffer from over-subtraction: the interarm regions are dominated by negative pixel values. To correct for this, the positive residual light (associated with the spiral-like features) is subtracted from the original galaxy image, producing an updated image in which the contribution of the spiral-like features is reduced. This updated image then re-enters the procedure, and the loop of smoothing, fitting, modeling, and subtracting is repeated until a convergence criterion is met. The iterations stop at the jump-out iteration (JOI), defined as the first iteration at which the median pixel value of the interarm region in the residual image reaches a value ≥ 0 \geq 0 , indicating that over-subtraction has been eliminated without introducing under-subtraction. A detailed, step-by-step description is given in Sect. 3 of Michea et al. (2021) . We note that the residual method differs from the unsharp masking, which is traditionally used to reveal substructure in dETGs ( Lisker et al., 2006a ; Lisker et al., 2006b , e.g.,) . In unsharp masking, the image is divided by, or has subtracted from it, a smoothed copy of itself using a kernel of fixed size; the technique is fast and effective at revealing where a feature is, but the amplitude of the enhanced structure depends on the kernel size in a way that has no direct photometric interpretation, and the smoothed copy is not a model of the diffuse component. The residual method instead builds an explicit axisymmetric model of the host from free-ellipticity isophote fit, the original spatial resolution is preserved,and the residual image is expressed in physical flux units and can be integrated to yield light fractions and, in the multiband extension used here, colors. The iterative loop additionally corrects for contamination of the model by the substructure light itself, the dominant systematic error of any single-pass subtraction. A more detailed comparison is given in Michea et al. (2021) . It is important to note that, throughout this work, the spiral-like feature refers to the nonaxisymmetric, excess light contained in the embedded substructures. It does not correspond to the total luminosity of a physically embedded spiral, which may also contribute a smooth component that is inseparable from the diffuse body of the galaxy ( Michea et al., 2021 ) . 3.1 Method setup The residual method has two free parameters common to both single-filter and multiband applications, plus one additional parameter specific to the multiband setup. The first parameter is the smoothing kernel size ( smooth ), which controls the standard deviation of the elliptical Gaussian kernel applied in the convolution step. Following Michea et al. (2021) , this size should match approximately half the average width of the spiral-like features, so that the substructures are effectively blurred out without significantly altering the overall galaxy geometry. For our sample we expressed this quantity in units of the PSF standard deviation ( σ PSF \sigma_{\mathrm{PSF}} ) and explored a range from 6 ​ σ PSF 6\,\sigma_{\mathrm{PSF}} to 12 ​ σ PSF 12\,\sigma_{\mathrm{PSF}} , stepped in increments of 1 ​ σ PSF 1\,\sigma_{\mathrm{PSF}} (seven values in total). As recommended by Michea et al. (2021) , the kernel size is halved after the first iteration, since the majority of the substructure light is removed in the initial pass and further smoothing should be kept to the minimum necessary to preserve the geometry of the diffuse component. The second parameter is the isophotal step size ( step-size ), which sets the geometric growth rate of the semimajor axis between consecutive isophotes during the ELLIPSE fitting. Smaller steps provide finer radial sampling of the light profile but require more data points per isophote; larger steps are more robust in low S/N regions but may miss subtle radial variations. We adopted a geometric growth rate ranging from 4 % 4\% to 10 % 10\% , also in increments of one percentage point (seven values). Together, the smoothing and step-size grids yield a total of 7 × 7 = 49 7\times 7=49 parameter combinations per galaxy. The third parameter, applicable only in the multiband setup, is the reference filter ( main-filter ). In a multiband analysis, the isophotal geometry must be derived in a single filter and then imposed on all other bands, so that the spatial decomposition is consistent across wavelengths ( Michea et al., 2022 ) . We adopted the i i band as the reference filter for all galaxies because of its greater depth. We first ran the full iterative procedure on the i i -band images and subsequently imposed the resulting isophotal geometry to the g g -band images to obtain the corresponding residual images. 3.2 A revised jump-out criterion The iterative nature of the residual method enables a progressively cleaner separation between embedded substructures and the diffuse component. In the implementation of Michea et al. (2021) , the convergence criterion monitors the median pixel value of an interarm region in the residual image, defined as all pixels that are negative in the first (pre iteration) residual and that lie within the 2 ​ R e 2\,R_{\mathrm{e}} isophote. As the iterations proceed, this region becomes less negative; the loop terminates once its median first reaches a value ≥ 0 \geq 0 , thereby avoiding both over- and under-subtraction. A limitation of this definition is that pixels that happen to have residual values ≥ 0 \geq 0 already in the first pass are permanently excluded from the interarm region and implicitly labeled as "arm" pixels, even when they are not associated with genuine spiral-like feature. While this mislabeling is often negligible in brighter systems, the low surface brightness and small angular size of the features in our targets motivate a stricter definition. We therefore retain the JOI framework of Michea et al. (2021) but focus on accurately identifying where the substructures are. Starting from an initial SExtractor segmentation map of the residual image, we applied a small set of morphological operations (erosion, dilation, and connected-component filtering; details in Appendix A ) designed to remove noise-driven detections and isolated mislabeled pixels while preserving contiguous spiral-arm footprints. The resulting arm measuring mask (AMM) provides a faithful delineation of the substructure regions. Its complement defines the interarm measuring mask (IAMM), which encompasses all nonarm pixels within the galaxy: a mixture of incompletely subtracted diffuse-component light and sky-level fluctuations. Because the IAMM now excludes spurious arm detections, it yields a more reliable estimate of the median nonarm level used to monitor convergence during the iterative loop. The main practical consequence of the revised criterion is that the iterative loop terminates ∼ \sim 2 iterations early, on average, than in the original implementation, so the final residual images contain less accumulated flux. This ensures that the photometric measurements of the arm and interarm regions are not contaminated by light from bright interlopers or by artifacts arising from the PSF-dominated core of the galaxy. 3.3 Residual results We applied the residual method to the g g - and i i -band images of nine Virgo dwarf galaxies from the NGVS.
